gloss_terse: sacrifices (Aramaic plural, ritual offerings in temple context)
gloss_readable: An Aramaic plural noun referring to ritual sacrifices offered in the Jerusalem temple. The term appears only in Ezra 6:3 in Cyrus's decree authorizing the reconstruction of the temple and the resumption of sacrificial worship. The multilingual glosses uniformly recognize this as the standard term for temple sacrifices, connecting to the broader semantic field of worship and offering in post-exilic restoration.

senses.1: The single occurrence in Ezra 6:3 appears in the administrative decree of Cyrus concerning temple reconstruction, where 'sacrifices' are mentioned as part of the authorized cultic activities. Spanish 'sacrificios' and English maintain the standard religious terminology, while French and German preserve the Aramaic form, highlighting the technical administrative nature of the decree.

gloss_terse: dove's dung (obscure term, possibly a plant name or literal excrement sold during famine)
gloss_readable: A disputed term appearing only in the dramatic famine account of 2 Kings 6:25, where basic commodities reached astronomical prices. The Hebrew is uncertain—the consonantal text suggests 'dove's dung,' though this may be a euphemism for an edible plant (perhaps a type of bulb or seed) or literally dried bird droppings used as fuel or salt substitute. The uncertainty is reflected in how translations handle it: some preserve the literal reading, while Arabic renders it descriptively.

senses.1: The lone occurrence in 2 Kings 6:25 describes Samaria's desperate siege conditions: 'dove's dung' sold for five shekels of silver. The parallel with 'donkey's head' (another famine food) suggests extreme scarcity. English and Spanish maintain the literal 'dove dung' reading, while Arabic explicitly marks this as excrement, and French/German preserve the Hebrew form, acknowledging the lexical uncertainty.

gloss_terse: Lidevir (place name in Gad's territory, east of Jordan, possibly identical with Lo-debar)
gloss_readable: A place name mentioned once in Joshua 13:26 as part of Gad's territorial boundary east of the Jordan. The text is difficult, and many scholars identify this with Lo-debar (mentioned in the David narratives). The Greek versions vary in their rendering, suggesting early uncertainty about the location. The name may mean 'no pasture' or 'no word,' fitting the semi-arid Transjordan landscape.

senses.1: The boundary description in Joshua 13:26 lists Lidevir as a landmark in Gad's allotment. Spanish interestingly reads 'Lo-Debar,' reflecting the scholarly consensus that these are variant names for the same site. English, French, and German preserve distinct forms, acknowledging the textual variation. The Septuagint's divergent transliterations suggest early geographical confusion about Transjordanian sites.

gloss_terse: Diblah (place name in Ezekiel, likely textual error for Riblah in Syria)
gloss_readable: A place name appearing in Ezekiel 6:14, though most scholars agree this is a scribal error for 'Riblah,' the well-known Syrian city that served as Nebuchadnezzar's military headquarters. The phrase 'from the wilderness to Diblah/Riblah' would describe the full extent of Israel's land from south to north. Modern commentaries uniformly prefer the Riblah reading, which makes better geographical and historical sense.

senses.1: In Ezekiel 6:14's oracle of judgment spanning 'from the wilderness to Diblah,' the context demands a northern boundary marker. Spanish renders this as 'Diblat,' French as 'Dibla,' while German preserves the consonantal Hebrew, all reflecting uncertainty. The emendation to 'Riblah' (a simple daleth/resh confusion) gives the expected north-south axis: southern wilderness to northern Syria.

gloss_terse: Diblaim (personal name, father of Gomer, Hosea's wife)
gloss_readable: The patronymic of Gomer, the unfaithful wife Hosea was commanded to marry as a living symbol of Israel's infidelity to Yahweh. The name appears only in Hosea 1:3 and may derive from a root meaning 'fig cakes,' possibly indicating the family's trade or origin. Like many names in Hosea 1-3, it may carry symbolic weight—'daughter of double cakes' suggesting indulgence or fertility cult associations.

senses.1: Hosea 1:3 identifies Gomer as 'daughter of Diblaim' in the controversial marriage command. The name appears uniformly across languages (English, Spanish: Diblaim; French: Diblah variant), with only German preserving Hebrew orthography. The symbolic onomastics of Hosea 1-3 (Lo-ruhamah, Lo-ammi) suggest this name too may signify more than mere identification, though its precise meaning remains debated.

gloss_terse: clinging (Aramaic participle, describing elements that fail to unite despite mixture)
gloss_readable: An Aramaic verbal participle in Daniel's vision of the fourth kingdom, describing how iron and clay 'cling' or 'adhere' to one another yet remain fundamentally incompatible. The image suggests political alliances or dynastic marriages that create superficial unity without genuine cohesion. The root is the same as Hebrew dabaq, which describes intimate bonding (Ruth cleaving to Naomi), making the image of failed clinging even more striking.

senses.1: Daniel 2:43 uses this participle in the vivid metaphor: 'they will cling together... but will not adhere to one another, just as iron does not mix with clay.' Spanish 'unidos' (united) and English 'clinging' capture the attempted but failed bonding. French 'coller' (to stick) emphasizes the adhesion metaphor. The multilingual consistency shows how translators recognize the ironic use of a bonding term for something that won't actually bond.

gloss_terse: and the word (disputed textual form in Jeremiah's prophetic critique)
gloss_readable: A grammatically difficult phrase in Jeremiah 5:13, where prophets are criticized as 'wind' with 'the word' not in them. The Hebrew text is obscure—it could be a noun with article ('and the word') or possibly a verbal form. Many scholars emend to 'the word' (without conjunction) for smoother syntax. The passage indicts false prophets who speak without divine authorization, making 'the word' (or lack thereof) thematically central.

senses.1: Jeremiah 5:13's biting critique says the prophets are 'wind, and the word is not in them.' The phrase structure is awkward, leading to various proposals. English, Spanish, French, and German all render it as 'and the word,' following the received text despite its difficulty. The theological point is clear across languages: these prophets speak their own ideas, not Yahweh's authoritative word (dabar).

gloss_terse: rafts (floats for transporting cedar logs from Lebanon by sea)
gloss_readable: A technical maritime term describing the log rafts used to transport Lebanese cedar from Hiram's Phoenician ports to Solomon's building projects. First Kings 5:9 describes Hiram's workers lashing logs together as rafts, floating them down the Mediterranean coast to the designated port, then breaking them apart for overland transport to Jerusalem. This was standard ancient Near Eastern practice for moving massive timber quantities.

senses.1: The logistics of Solomon's temple project required innovative transport: 1 Kings 5:9 explains that Hiram 'will make them into rafts to go by sea to the place you indicate.' Spanish 'en balsas' (in rafts) and English agree on the floating log-raft method. The term appears only here, reflecting specialized maritime vocabulary for this timber-export industry that was Phoenicia's economic backbone.

gloss_terse: from your words (poetic term for divine instruction received from Moses)
gloss_readable: A rare poetic word appearing in Moses's blessing of Levi (Deuteronomy 33:3), describing how the tribes receive divine words or instruction. The phrase 'he receives from your words' suggests the people gathering at Moses's feet to hear Torah. The term is a poetic variant of the common dabar (word), lending elevated tone to this archaic blessing poem. All translations recognize this as referring to Moses's authoritative teaching.

senses.1: Deuteronomy 33:3's dense poetry says the people are 'at your feet, receiving from your words.' The preposition-plus-noun construction ('from your words') is rendered consistently: Spanish 'de tus palabras,' French 'de ton paroles,' German 'von dein Worte,' all capturing the image of instruction flowing from Moses to Israel. The poetic vocabulary elevates the ordinary 'word' to covenant instruction.

gloss_terse: Dibri (personal name, a Danite, father of Shelomith whose son was stoned for blasphemy)
gloss_readable: The father of Shelomith, the Israelite woman whose son (by an Egyptian father) blasphemed the divine Name and was stoned in the wilderness narrative of Leviticus 24. The name Dibri appears only in this context, marking the maternal lineage of the blasphemer since his father was not Israelite. The incident establishes case law for blasphemy punishment and the status of mixed parentage in the covenant community.

senses.1: Leviticus 24:11 identifies the blasphemer as 'son of Shelomith daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.' The name is uniform across translations (English, Spanish, French, German all: Dibri), serving primarily as genealogical identification. The detail of maternal lineage is unusual and emphasizes the son's ambiguous status—Israelite mother, Egyptian father—which may relate to why the case required judicial clarification.

gloss_terse: the humps (of camels, part of description of caravan bearing wealth through desert)
gloss_readable: A rare anatomical term for camel humps, appearing in Isaiah's oracle against Egypt and Ethiopia (Isaiah 30:6). The prophet envisions a desperate caravan carrying tribute through the dangerous Negev: wealth loaded 'on the humps of camels.' The image emphasizes both the hazard of the journey and the futility of trusting Egypt. The word is related to a place name (Dabbesheth), suggesting possible connection to local geography or camel-breeding areas.

senses.1: Isaiah 30:6 paints a vivid scene: 'they carry their riches on the humps of camels, their treasures on the backs of donkeys.' English and Spanish recognize the anatomical term ('humps,' 'joroba de'), while French and German preserve the Hebrew, possibly unsure of the rare vocabulary. The camel hump as load-bearer is culturally specific imagery from desert trade routes.

gloss_terse: in Dabbesheth (place name, a boundary town in Zebulun's allotment)
gloss_readable: A town on Zebulun's border mentioned once in the tribal allotment (Joshua 19:11). The site has not been conclusively identified, though it lay in the western part of Zebulun's territory. The name may be related to 'hump' or possibly a topographical feature. The boundary descriptions in Joshua 13-19 preserve ancient geographical knowledge, many details of which remain obscure.

senses.1: Joshua 19:11 traces Zebulun's border: 'their boundary goes up westward... to Dabbesheth.' The prepositional phrase ('in/at Dabbesheth') is consistent across languages: Spanish 'en Dabeset,' English 'in Dabbesheth,' French and German matching. The term functions purely as geographical reference in the technical boundary list, its etymology secondary to its role as a landmark.

gloss_terse: and let them multiply (jussive verb, Jacob's blessing that Ephraim and Manasseh increase like fish)
gloss_readable: A verbal form in Jacob's blessing over Joseph's sons (Genesis 48:16), invoking fruitfulness using an unusual verb related to fish (dag). The phrase 'let them multiply like fish' (or 'teem/swarm') evokes the creation blessing and connects to Jacob's own name-giving—his descendants will multiply abundantly in the land. The imagery is uniquely aquatic, perhaps reflecting Egypt's Nile-based fertility or simply emphasizing prolific reproduction.

senses.1: Genesis 48:16 concludes Jacob's blessing: 'may they multiply greatly in the midst of the land.' The verb is from the root for 'fish,' suggesting swarming abundance. Spanish 'multiplíquense' and English 'let them multiply' recognize the jussive mood. German 'sie sollen wimmeln' (they shall swarm/teem) captures the fish imagery more explicitly. The multilingual consensus is on rapid, fish-like population growth.

gloss_terse: distinguished (passive participle, describing the beloved as conspicuous among many)
gloss_readable: A disputed term in Song of Songs 5:10, where the woman describes her beloved as 'distinguished among ten thousand.' The root may mean 'to look at, behold' (thus 'conspicuous, looked-upon') or be denominative from 'banner/standard' (thus 'exalted, pre-eminent'). Either way, the sense is clear: he stands out from the crowd. The multilingual glosses show translators opting for 'distinguished' without committing to a specific etymology.

senses.1: In the bride's lavish description (Song 5:10), she begins: 'My beloved is radiant and distinguished among ten thousand.' The participle suggests being singled out, conspicuous. English, Spanish, and French all choose 'distinguished/distingué,' avoiding the etymological debate. The context of the catalog of his perfections makes pre-eminence the key idea, however the word's origin is understood.

gloss_terse: Dedan (place/people name, Arabian trading group, likely a textual variant for Rhodes in Ezekiel 27)
gloss_readable: A name occurring in Ezekiel 27:15's catalog of Tyre's trading partners, though many scholars believe this is a scribal error for 'Rhodes' (Hebrew consonants are similar). If the traditional reading 'Dedan' is retained, it refers to the Arabian trading people mentioned elsewhere as dealing in saddle blankets and other goods. The uncertainty reflects how Ezekiel 27's trade list preserves ancient commercial geography that sometimes challenges later scribes.

senses.1: Ezekiel 27:15 lists Tyre's clients: 'The men of Dedan traded with you.' All four languages preserve 'Dedan,' though modern commentaries often read 'Rhodes' based on Greek versions. The confusion is understandable: both were maritime traders, and the consonantal Hebrew differs by only one letter. The multilingual uniformity reflects the traditional Masoretic text rather than the emendation.

gloss_terse: Dedanites (gentilic plural, Arabian trading caravans addressed in Isaiah's oracle)
gloss_readable: The plural demonym for people of Dedan, an Arabian trading group, mentioned in Isaiah 21:13. The oracle addresses 'caravans of Dedanites' camping in the desert thickets, warning them of coming disaster. Dedan was a significant north Arabian trading center, and its merchants trafficked in luxury goods along the incense route. Isaiah's reference captures the disruption of normal commerce during times of military upheaval.

senses.1: Isaiah 21:13 directly addresses 'O caravans of Dedanites' (literally 'traveling companies of Dedanites'), warning them to bring water to the fugitives. English and Spanish recognize the ethnic designation, while French and German preserve the Hebrew form. The context is Arabian trading networks disrupted by war, with Dedan representing the merchant caravans that would normally traverse these routes.

gloss_terse: Dehaye (uncertain ethnic/place name in Ezra's list of Persian officials, possibly meaning 'that is')
gloss_readable: An obscure term in Ezra 4:9's list of Persian officials who opposed Jerusalem's reconstruction. The text is uncertain—it may be an ethnic designation, a title, or even the Aramaic phrase 'that is' serving as a clarifying particle. The Greek renders it as 'who are,' supporting the explanatory reading. This illustrates the textual and historical difficulties in Ezra's administrative correspondence, which preserves Persian-period terminology often opaque to later readers.

senses.1: Ezra 4:9 catalogues the opponents: 'the judges, the officials, the Dehaye...' Spanish renders this interpretively as '(los dehitas)' (the Dehaites), treating it as an ethnic group. English 'Dehaye' and German preserve the uncertain term. The Greek's 'who are' suggests this may not be a people-group at all but an Aramaic connector. The multilingual variation reveals the text's resistance to clear interpretation.

gloss_terse: bewildered (niphal participle, describing a warrior too stunned to act)
gloss_readable: A participial form in Jeremiah 14:9 comparing Yahweh's apparent inaction to 'a man bewildered, a warrior unable to save.' The root conveys being stunned, confused, or paralyzed with astonishment. The prophet uses it in his anguished prayer during drought, questioning why God seems helpless. The image is deliberately shocking—Yahweh compared to a dazed, incapacitated soldier—reflecting the prayer's raw emotion.

senses.1: Jeremiah 14:9's bold simile asks, 'Why should you be like a man bewildered, like a warrior who cannot save?' Spanish 'aturdido' (stunned, dazed) captures the sense well. The context is God's apparent passivity during national crisis. The root suggests being struck dumb with shock. French and German preserve the Hebrew, possibly uncertain of this rare vocabulary, while English and Spanish grasp the paralysis imagery.

gloss_terse: galloping (participle, describing the rushing of warhorses in battle)
gloss_readable: An onomatopoetic participle capturing the sound and motion of charging cavalry in Nahum's vision of Nineveh's fall (Nahum 3:2). The word conveys the thundering rush of horses at full gallop, contributing to the passage's vivid soundscape of battle: cracking whips, rumbling wheels, galloping horses. The term appears only here, its sound (doher) suggesting the drumbeat of hooves. Ancient readers likely heard the word's sonic force.

senses.1: Nahum 3:2 piles up battle sounds: 'The crack of whip! The rumble of wheel! Galloping horse!' Spanish adds an exclamation point ('galopando!'), matching the staccato Hebrew. French 'galoper' and English 'galloping' capture the rushing motion. The participial form suggests continuous action—this is the chaotic soundscape of urban warfare, with cavalry pounding through streets in Nineveh's final hours.

gloss_terse: and causing soul to pine (hiphil participle, diseases that waste away the life force)
gloss_readable: A participial phrase in the Levitical curses (Leviticus 26:16) describing diseases that cause the soul or life to waste away. The imagery is of consumption, wasting illness that drains vitality. The hiphil causative form emphasizes that these afflictions actively produce the wasting effect—they're not mere sickness but life-destroying plagues. The covenant curses use visceral, physical imagery to depict covenant breakdown's consequences.

senses.1: Leviticus 26:16 threatens disobedient Israel: 'I will bring upon you... diseases causing the soul to pine away.' Spanish 'hacen languidecer' (they make languish/waste) captures the causative sense well. The phrase combines 'soul' (nephesh, life-force) with wasting verbs, suggesting consumptive diseases. English, French, and German all preserve the 'soul/life pining away' imagery, recognizing this as terminal illness, not mere discomfort.

gloss_terse: of fish (construct noun in phrase 'boats of fishing,' describing fish transport vessels)
gloss_readable: A term in Amos 4:2's metaphor for Israel's coming captivity, where Yahweh promises to take them away 'in boats of fishing' (or 'fish boats,' 'fishing vessels'). The imagery is of fish being hauled off in fishermen's boats, a humiliating comparison for captured people. The parallel line mentions 'hooks,' completing the fishing metaphor. The phrase appears only here, making its precise nuance uncertain—is it boats used for fishing, or boats for transporting fish?

senses.1: Amos 4:2 warns Samaria's elite women: 'They will take you away... in boats of fishing.' Spanish 'pesca' (fishing) recognizes the maritime imagery. The context suggests fish-transport rather than fishing boats per se—the people themselves are the catch being hauled away. French 'pêche' and English 'of fish' maintain the construct relationship. The metaphor reduces proud nobles to dead fish in fishmongers' boats.

gloss_terse: Dodavahu (personal name meaning 'beloved of Yahweh,' father of the prophet Eliezer)
gloss_readable: A theophoric personal name appearing once (2 Chronicles 20:37), identifying the father of Eliezer who prophesied against Jehoshaphat's ill-fated alliance with Ahaziah. The name means 'beloved of Yahweh' or 'Yahweh loves,' a common onomastic pattern. The Septuagint variants show uncertainty about the exact form, but the theophoric element is clear. The prophet's message proved true when the joint naval venture shipwrecked.

senses.1: Second Chronicles 20:37 introduces the prophet: 'Eliezer son of Dodavahu of Mareshah.' Spanish shortens to 'Dodava,' while French and German preserve the fuller Hebrew orthography. The name's meaning ('Yah's beloved') is ironic given that his son prophesies against the king's policy. Across languages, the name functions as pure identification, its etymology secondary to its role in validating Eliezer's credentials.

gloss_terse: Dodai (personal name, variant of Dodo, an officer in David's administration)
gloss_readable: A variant form of the name Dodo, appearing in 1 Chronicles 27:4 to identify one of David's military division commanders. The name means 'his beloved' or perhaps 'beloved one.' This is the same person called Dodo in other lists of David's mighty men, showing the fluidity of Hebrew spelling in proper names. The Chronicler's administrative lists preserve this variant form.

senses.1: First Chronicles 27:4 lists 'Dodai the Ahohite' as one of the twelve monthly division commanders. The name appears uniformly in most languages (English, Spanish: Dodai), with French and German preserving Hebrew spelling. The context is bureaucratic—monthly roster of 24,000-man divisions. The name's root meaning ('beloved') is common in Hebrew onomastics, marking family affection rather than theological claim.

gloss_terse: her sickness (construct infinitive, referring to menstrual impurity period)
gloss_readable: An infinitive construct in Leviticus 12:2, part of the purity laws concerning childbirth. The phrase 'in the days of her sickness of her impurity' refers to the menstrual period, using 'sickness' (davah) as a euphemism for the monthly flow considered ritually unclean. The text establishes that a woman after childbirth has similar impurity status to her menstrual period. The terminology is clinical, using standard priestly vocabulary for ritual states.

senses.1: Leviticus 12:2 sets the baseline: 'she shall be unclean as in the days of her sickness of her impurity.' Spanish 'su enfermedad' (her sickness), French 'sa maladie,' and German 'ihr Krankheit' all preserve the euphemistic 'sickness' terminology for menstruation. The consistency across languages shows how translators recognize the priestly idiom for ritual impurity, not actual illness.

gloss_terse: beat (qal perfect, pounding grain in a mortar)
gloss_readable: A verb describing the processing of manna in the wilderness (Numbers 11:8). The people would gather it, then either grind it with millstones or pound it in a mortar before cooking. The term denotes the percussive action of pestle against mortar, crushing the grain-like substance. This parallels ancient food preparation techniques still used for spices and grains. The mundane detail grounds the miraculous manna in actual culinary practice.

senses.1: Numbers 11:8 describes manna preparation: 'The people... ground it in mills or beat it in a mortar.' The verb appears in parallel with 'grind,' differentiating two processing methods. Spanish 'machacaron' (they pounded/crushed) captures the percussive action. English 'beat' and the uniform verb across languages suggests everyone recognized this as mortar-and-pestle work, turning the flaky manna into flour or paste for baking.

gloss_terse: leaps (qal imperfect, describing anguish dancing or skipping before the fearsome creature)
gloss_readable: A verb in Job's description of Leviathan (Job 41:22), where even terror or anguish 'dances' or 'leaps' before this fearsome creature. The image is striking: not that terror flees, but that it cavorts or gambles before Leviathan, perhaps suggesting that even fear itself becomes playful or frantic in his presence. The root suggests rhythmic movement—dancing, leaping, perhaps trembling. This is part of Job 41's sustained portrait of Leviathan's overwhelming power.

senses.1: Job 41:22 (English 41:14) says 'before him dances anguish.' Spanish 'salta' (leaps/jumps) and English 'leaps' capture the kinetic energy. The verb conveys sudden, erratic movement—terror doesn't just exist near Leviathan but performs a kind of frenzied dance. French and German preserve the Hebrew, possibly uncertain of this rare poetic vocabulary. The image contributes to the passage's hyperbolic depiction of the chaos creature.

gloss_terse: rather than dwell (qal infinitive in comparative construction, choosing temple service over wickedness)
gloss_readable: An infinitive in Psalm 84:10, expressing the psalmist's preference: 'I would rather stand at the threshold of God's house than dwell in the tents of wickedness.' The verb is from the root for 'dwell, sojourn,' here in a comparative construction. The statement prioritizes even lowly temple service (doorkeeping) over comfortable residence among the wicked. The sentiment reflects the psalm's broader theme: longing for God's presence exceeds all other values.

senses.1: Psalm 84:10 makes the famous declaration: 'I would rather be a doorkeeper... than dwell in the tents of wickedness.' Spanish 'que morar' (than to dwell) and French 'de séjourner' both preserve the dwelling/sojourning sense. The infinitival form in a comparison clause appears consistently across languages. The theological point—proximity to God trumps worldly comfort—resonates across the translations.

gloss_terse: like the ball (simile marker + noun, describing exile as being hurled like a ball into distance)
gloss_readable: A prepositional phrase in Isaiah 22:18, where Yahweh promises to hurl Shebna 'like a ball' into a broad land. The image is of violent, spinning ejection—Shebna will be thrown away like a child's toy or athletic implement, tumbling helplessly into foreign exile. The simile captures both the violence and the contemptuous dismissal. The word may also mean 'circle' or 'sphere,' but the context supports the ball imagery.

senses.1: Isaiah 22:18 pronounces judgment on the steward Shebna: 'He will surely wind you round and round, and throw you like a ball into a wide land.' Spanish 'como pelota' (like a ball) and English preserve the simile. The Hebrew's brevity ('like-the-ball') is maintained across languages, emphasizing the ignominious image of being hurled away like a plaything.

gloss_terse: Dura (place name, plain near Babylon where Nebuchadnezzar erected the golden image)
gloss_readable: A place name in Daniel 3:1, identifying the location where Nebuchadnezzar set up the massive golden image for forced worship. The 'plain of Dura' was somewhere in the Babylonian province, though the exact site is unknown. Several places in Mesopotamia bore similar names (related to 'wall' or 'enclosure' in Akkadian). The narrative emphasizes the public, accessible location—a plain where all officials could assemble.

senses.1: Daniel 3:1 sets the scene: 'Nebuchadnezzar... set up the image on the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon.' English, Spanish, and most languages preserve 'Dura' uniformly. The Septuagint's 'of the enclosure' may reflect etymological interpretation. The narrative function is clear: this is a grand public space for the coerced worship ceremony that will test the three Jewish youths.

gloss_terse: and tread it down (Aramaic qal consecutive imperfect with suffix, beast trampling the earth)
gloss_readable: An Aramaic verbal form in Daniel's vision of the fourth beast (Daniel 7:23), describing how it will 'tread down' or 'trample' the whole earth. The verb conveys violent crushing underfoot, fitting the beast's destructive character. The feminine suffix refers to 'the earth,' making this a picture of global domination through brutal force. The imagery of trampling echoes ancient Near Eastern conquest metaphors.

senses.1: Daniel 7:23 interprets the vision: 'The fourth beast... shall devour the whole earth, tread it down, and break it in pieces.' Spanish 'la trillará' (will thresh/trample it) and French 'fouler' (to trample) capture the agricultural trampling imagery. The suffix 'it' (the earth) is consistent across languages. The verb's violence matches the beast's iron teeth and bronze claws—total, crushing domination.

gloss_terse: they will be driven (niphal imperfect, the wicked thrust down in darkness)
gloss_readable: A niphal imperfect verb in Jeremiah 23:12, describing how the wicked's path will become slippery darkness and 'they will be driven' or 'thrust down' into it. The passive form suggests divine judgment—they don't merely slip but are pushed. The text may be emended from this rare root to the more common dachah (drive out), but the sense remains: forcible removal into danger and darkness as punishment for false prophecy.

senses.1: Jeremiah 23:12 threatens false prophets: 'Their way shall be to them like slippery paths in the darkness; they will be driven on and fall in it.' Spanish 'serán empujados' (they will be pushed/driven) captures the forcible propulsion. The passive voice appears uniformly—these prophets won't accidentally slip but will be thrust down. French and German preserve the Hebrew, acknowledging textual uncertainty while maintaining the judgment imagery.

gloss_terse: and entertainment (Aramaic plural noun, uncertain meaning, possibly music, dancing, or concubines)
gloss_readable: An obscure Aramaic plural noun in Daniel 6:18, describing something King Darius rejected during his anxious night while Daniel was in the lions' den. Ancient and modern interpreters disagree: musical instruments? Dancing girls? Concubines? Food and entertainment generally? The Septuagint and other versions guessed variously. The context suggests diversions or comforts the king refused in his distress, but the precise meaning remains elusive.

senses.1: Daniel 6:18 says Darius 'spent the night fasting; no entertainment was brought before him, and sleep fled from him.' Spanish 'diversiones' (entertainments) and English 'entertainment' take the broadest interpretive path. French retains 'fouler' (trample—likely a database error), while German preserves the Hebrew, acknowledging lexical uncertainty. The narrative point is clear: Darius rejected all comfort in solidarity with Daniel's peril.

gloss_terse: and millet (grain type in Ezekiel's symbolic bread recipe during siege)
gloss_readable: A grain type mentioned in Ezekiel 4:9's list of ingredients for the prophet's siege bread. Millet was a common ancient Near Eastern grain, drought-resistant and nutritious but considered inferior to wheat. The mix of wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt represents scavenging whatever grains were available during food scarcity—normally, these wouldn't be combined. The recipe symbolizes the desperation of Jerusalem's coming siege.

senses.1: Ezekiel 4:9 commands: 'Take wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt; put them into one vessel and make bread of them.' Spanish 'mijo,' French 'mil,' and English 'millet' all identify this grain uniformly. The context is famine food—mixing diverse grains that would normally be kept separate. Millet's inclusion shows the extremity: even less desirable grains must be used to survive the siege.

gloss_terse: and they will fish them (qal perfect consecutive with suffix, hunters pursuing scattered Israel)
gloss_readable: A verbal form in Jeremiah 16:16, where Yahweh promises to send 'fishermen' who will 'fish them' (the scattered Israelites), followed by hunters who will hunt them from every mountain and hill. The fishing metaphor suggests capture and gathering, here with ominous overtones—these fishermen work for judgment, not rescue. The verb may be qal or an abbreviated hiphil, but the sense is clear: systematic searching and seizing of the exiled people.

senses.1: Jeremiah 16:16 uses vivid imagery: 'I will send for many fishermen, and they will fish them out. Afterward I will send for many hunters, and they will hunt them.' Spanish 'los pescarán' (they will fish them) and English preserve the metaphor. The suffix 'them' (Israel) is consistent. The double image—fishing then hunting—suggests comprehensive, inescapable pursuit of the people in exile, whether for judgment or eventual restoration.

gloss_terse: with the ink (prepositional phrase, Baruch's writing medium for Jeremiah's scroll)
gloss_readable: A prepositional phrase in Jeremiah 36:18, describing how Baruch wrote Jeremiah's dictated prophecies. When questioned about the scroll's production, Baruch explained that Jeremiah spoke the words and 'I wrote them with ink on the scroll.' The detail emphasizes the physical, documentary nature of prophetic preservation—these are not oral traditions but written records. Ancient Hebrew ink was typically carbon-based (soot mixed with gum or oil), erasable when fresh.

senses.1: Jeremiah 36:18 records Baruch's testimony: 'He dictated all these words to me, and I wrote them with ink on the scroll.' Spanish 'con la tinta' and English 'with the ink' preserve the instrumental prepositional phrase. The mundane detail grounds the prophetic word in scribal practice—real ink, real parchment, real dictation. The ink's erasable quality becomes significant later when the king burns the scroll.

gloss_terse: and Di-zahab (place name meaning 'of gold,' location of Moses's final address to Israel)
gloss_readable: A place name in the geographical heading of Deuteronomy (1:1), locating Moses's farewell address 'in the wilderness... opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel and Laban and Hazeroth and Di-zahab.' The name means 'sufficient gold' or 'of gold,' though the site is unidentified. The Septuagint renders it as 'Gold-place.' This is part of Deuteronomy's complex geographical preamble, marking where Moses stood to review Israel's history.

senses.1: Deuteronomy 1:1 sets the scene with multiple landmarks, including 'and Di-zahab.' The conjunction-plus-name structure appears uniformly: Spanish 'y Di-Zahab,' French 'et Di-Zahab,' German 'und Di-Zahab.' All preserve the hyphenated transliteration. The name's meaning ('of gold') is preserved in the Septuagint's translation. Its function is purely geographical—one of several sites triangulating Moses's location in Transjordan.

gloss_terse: and Dimonah (place name in southern Judah, possibly identical with Dibon)
gloss_readable: A town in Judah's southern allotment (Joshua 15:22), possibly identical to Dibon mentioned elsewhere in Negev contexts. The name appears only here, and the site is unidentified. The similarity to Dibon (and Isaiah's Dimon) suggests these may be variant spellings of the same settlement, though the geographical contexts differ (Moabite Dibon vs. Judahite Dimonah). The boundary lists preserve archaic place names, many now lost.

senses.1: Joshua 15:22 lists towns in southern Judah's inheritance: 'Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah...' Spanish renders 'y Dimoná,' English 'and Dimonah,' French and German matching. The conjunction-plus-name pattern is consistent. The name's obscurity and single occurrence mean translations simply transliterate without interpretive comment. Its connection to other 'Dibon/Dimon' names remains scholarly speculation.

gloss_terse: and judges (Aramaic plural noun, legal officials in Artaxerxes's authorization to Ezra)
gloss_readable: An Aramaic plural noun in Artaxerxes's decree (Ezra 7:25), authorizing Ezra to appoint magistrates and judges to administer Jewish law in the Trans-Euphrates province. The term appears in parallel with 'those who know the laws of your God,' indicating legal functionaries who would adjudicate according to Torah. This represents Persian imperial policy of allowing subject peoples judicial autonomy under their ancestral laws.

senses.1: Ezra 7:25 records the royal authorization: 'Appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people in Trans-Euphrates.' Spanish 'y jueces' (and judges) and English maintain the straightforward plural. The Aramaic form is recognizable across languages. The context is legal administration—Ezra may establish a Torah-based court system with Persian backing, showing the empire's pragmatic delegation of local governance.

gloss_terse: Dinaye (uncertain term in Ezra 4:9, possibly ethnic name or reading 'judges' as Persian title)
gloss_readable: An obscure term in Ezra 4:9's list of Persian officials opposing Jerusalem's reconstruction. It may be an ethnic designation, a Persian title meaning 'judges' (from an Iranian word for judicial officers), or part of the preceding word. Modern scholarship divides on whether to read this as a people-group (Dinaites) or as an Aramaic/Persian administrative term. The textual difficulty reflects the complexities of Persian-period administrative vocabulary.

senses.1: Ezra 4:9 lists the opposition: 'the judges... the Dinaye, the Apharsathchites...' Spanish reads 'los jueces' (the judges), treating this as the Aramaic word for judicial officials rather than an ethnic name. English 'Dinaye' and German preserve the uncertain term. The scholarly debate whether this is a Persian loan-word or a proper noun is reflected in the divergent translations—Spanish opts for the functional reading.

gloss_terse: threshing (noun, the process of threshing grain, in promise of agricultural abundance)
gloss_readable: A noun describing the threshing process, appearing in Leviticus 26:5's promise of agricultural blessing: 'your threshing shall last until grape harvest, and grape harvest until sowing time.' The image is of such abundant crops that processing the grain takes months, overlapping with the next season's work. Threshing involved oxen or sledges crushing grain to separate kernels from chaff. The promise reverses the covenant curses of crop failure.

senses.1: Leviticus 26:5 paints prosperity: 'Your threshing will continue until grape harvest, and the grape harvest will continue until planting.' Spanish 'la trilla' and English 'threshing' identify the grain-processing phase. The blessing is temporal overlap—so much wheat that threshing season extends abnormally long, bumping into vintage season. This is covenant abundance: labor's blessing of plenty rather than the curse of scarcity.
